claims.claim: Going to a holy place can bring you closer to God.

stances.summary: Moving from one place to another does not bring you any nearer to God. God comes to you wherever you are, if your soul is a place He can live in. Praise Him where you are instead of travelling to Palestine.
stances.quote: Change of place does not effect any drawing nearer unto God, but wherever you may be, God will come to you, if the chambers of your soul be found of such a sort that He can dwell in you and walk in you.
stances.translation: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson, NPNF second series vol. 5, 1893
stances.location: the whole short letter; this line near the end
stances.context: A whole letter written to argue this, so strength 2. Written after his own journey to Arabia and Jerusalem in the early 380s, which he says he made only on church business, in an imperial post-waggon. His reasons: Christ never listed a pilgrimage among the good works that win the kingdom or among the Beatitudes; the journey endangers modesty, especially for women monastics, in the inns of the East; Jerusalem is full of crime, so grace is not more abundant there; and seeing Bethlehem, the Tomb and the Mount of Olives added nothing to his faith. Same letter: 'He cannot imagine that our Lord is living, in the body, there at the present day'. He addresses monks and nuns ('those who have dedicated themselves once for all to the higher life'), not all Christians. Nuance: in another letter he says he was filled with joy at seeing the holy places, but at once moves the holy places into the heart: 'When, then, I not only saw with the sense of sight those Sacred Places, but I saw the tokens of places like them, plain in yourselves as well, I was filled with joy so great that the description of its blessing is beyond the power of utterance' (NPNF Letter 17, Letter 3 in modern editions, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/291117.htm). His homily on the martyr Theodore is widely cited as praising visits to a martyr's shrine; not checked for this file. Authenticity: Reformation-era Protestants printed the letter against pilgrimage and some Catholic controversialists questioned whether it was his; modern editors accept it as Gregory's. Fully orthodox.

stances.summary: Worshipping where the Lord's feet stood is part of a believer's faith. Seeing the places of His birth, cross and passion is worth the journey.
stances.quote: Even supposing that you do not care for our society, it is still your duty as believers to worship on the spot where the Lord's feet once stood and to see for yourselves the still fresh traces of His birth, His cross, and His passion.
stances.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, NPNF second series vol. 6, 1893
stances.original: certe, si consortia displicuerint, adorasse, ubi steterunt pedes domini, pars fidei est et quasi recentia natiuitatis et crucis ac passionis uidisse uestigia.
stances.context: Jerome's own voice, written from Bethlehem in 393, inviting friends from Rome. The Latin says literally 'it is a part of faith' (pars fidei est) to have worshipped where the Lord's feet stood; NPNF renders it 'duty as believers'. Latin from Hilberg, CSEL 54 (1910), read in the archive.org OCR text https://archive.org/download/corpusscriptorum54stuoft/corpusscriptorum54stuoft_djvu.txt (line breaks and hyphens removed). Earlier, Letter 46 (386), written by Jerome in the names of Paula and Eustochium to Marcella, argues the same at length: bishops, martyrs and scholars came to Jerusalem 'from a feeling that their devotion and knowledge would be incomplete and their virtue without the finishing touch, unless they adored Christ in the very spot where the gospel first flashed from the gibbet', and it asks 'can we suppose a Christian's education complete who has not visited the Christian Athens?' (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3001046.htm, section 9). Letter 46 also says 'we do not mean to deny that the kingdom of God is within us'. Two years after Letter 47 he wrote Letter 58 (see the next entry), which cools this sharply. Later still he praised Paula's devotion at the holy places at length (Letter 108, AD 404) and defended honouring martyrs' tombs against Vigilantius (406). He lived in Bethlehem from 386 until his death.

stances.summary: You lose nothing by never seeing Jerusalem, and living there has not made me better. Heaven is as close from Britain as from Jerusalem, because the kingdom of God is within you. What counts is not having been to Jerusalem but living well.
stances.quote: To assure you that nothing is lacking to your faith although you have not seen Jerusalem and that I am none the better for living where I do.
stances.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, NPNF second series vol. 6, 1893
stances.original: uidelicet ne quicquam fidei tuae deesse putes, quia Hierosolymam non uidisti, nec nos idcirco meliores aestimes, quod huius loci habitaculo fruimur
stances.location: Letter 58, sections 2 to 4 (about AD 395); this line opens section 4
stances.context: A change of emphasis from Letter 47 (393), not a lasting reversal. Written to dissuade Paulinus, a monk, from coming. Nearby lines on the same page: 'What is praiseworthy is not to have been at Jerusalem but to have lived a good life while there' (section 2) and 'Access to the courts of heaven is as easy from Britain as it is from Jerusalem; for the kingdom of God is within you' (section 3; Latin 'et de Hierosolymis et de Britannia aequaliter patet aula caelestis; regnum enim dei intra nos est'). He notes that Antony and the monks of Egypt never saw Jerusalem, and that Hilarion saw it only once, 'not wishing on the one hand when he was so near to neglect the holy places, nor yet on the other to appear to confine God within local limits'. Qualifications, so strength 1: he says he is not condemning his own choice to live there; 'the spots which witnessed the crucifixion and the resurrection profit those only who bear their several crosses, who day by day rise again with Christ'; and much of his reason is that Jerusalem is a crowded city, bad for a monk. Latin from Hilberg, CSEL 54, archive.org OCR text (see previous entry; a margin line number 'io' splits 'Hieroso-lymam' there).

stances.summary: To kiss the manger and pray in the cave where Christ was born is a gift beyond deserving. This is where I will rest, because my Saviour chose this place. I cannot find another Bethlehem anywhere else.
stances.quote: I too, miserable sinner though I am, have been accounted worthy to kiss the manger in which the Lord cried as a babe, and to pray in the cave in which the travailing virgin gave birth to the infant Lord. This is my rest for it is my Lord's native place; here will I dwell for this spot has my Saviour chosen.
stances.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, NPNF second series vol. 6, 1893
stances.original: et ego, misera atque peccatrix, digna sum iudicata deosculari praesepe, in quo dominus paruulus uagiit, orare in spelunca, in qua uirgo puerpera deum fudit infantem? haec requies mea, quia domini mei patria est. hic habitabo, quoniam saluator elegit eam.
stances.context: Paula (347 to 404), a Roman noblewoman, Jerome's patron and fellow scholar; not in the candidate pool, recorded because her words are preserved by an eyewitness. Jerome writes that at Bethlehem 'she protested in my hearing' that she could see with the eyes of faith the infant Lord in the manger, then records her speech, of which this is the end. So it is a near-contemporary record of her words, written by her closest friend shortly after her death, and polished by him. Same letter, section 18, when Jerome advised her to leave Bethlehem to escape an enemy, she answered: 'Moreover, I am deterred from accepting it by my love for the holy places; and I cannot find another Bethlehem elsewhere.' Section 9 describes her at the Cross and the Tomb: 'Before the Cross she threw herself down in adoration as though she beheld the Lord hanging upon it'. Latin from Hilberg, CSEL 55 (1912), archive.org OCR text https://archive.org/download/corpusscriptorum55stuoft/corpusscriptorum55stuoft_djvu.txt (OCR 'fudir' corrected to 'fudit').

stances.summary: At every holy place we reached we prayed, read the Bible passage that happened there, sang a fitting psalm and prayed again. The toil of the journey is no toil when you see your desire fulfilled.
stances.quote: For it was always customary with us that, whenever we succeeded in reaching the places we desired to visit, prayer should first be made there, then the lection should be read from the book, then one appropriate psalm should be said, then prayer should be made again.
stances.translation: M.L. McClure and C.L. Feltoe, The Pilgrimage of Etheria, SPCK, 1919
stances.original: Id enim nobis semper consuetudinis erat, ut ubicumque ad loca desiderata accedere volebamus, primum ibi fieret oratio, deinde legeretur lectio ipsa de codice, diceretur etiam psalmus unus pertinens ad rem et iterato fieret ibi oratio.
stances.work: Travels (Itinerarium Egeriae; McClure calls her Etheria)
stances.context: Not in the candidate pool; recorded as the fullest early witness. A woman from the far West (Gaul or Spain) who spent about three years (around 381 to 384) visiting the holy places and writing home to her 'sisters'. The whole work is the stance, so strength 2. Same page: she went to Job's tomb 'for the sake of prayer', after seeing many holy monks come 'to Jerusalem to visit the holy places for the sake of prayer', and calls it a toil 'if indeed that can be called toil by which a man sees his desire to be fulfilled'. She never argues the point; she simply assumes that prayer at the place, with the Scripture read on the spot, is worth the journey. Latin from The Latin Library, https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/egeria1.html (line breaks removed).

stances.summary: Other Christians only hear the story, but we who stand at Golgotha see and touch it. The places themselves are witnesses to Christ.
stances.quote: And yet we never can be tired of hearing concerning the crowning of our Lord, and least of all in this most holy Golgotha. For others only hear, but we both see and handle.
stances.translation: Edwin Hamilton Gifford, NPNF second series vol. 7, 1894
stances.context: Not in the candidate pool. Bishop of Jerusalem; the lectures were given to baptismal candidates around 350 in the church built over Golgotha. He returns to the theme again and again, so strength 2: Lecture 10.19 lists witnesses to Christ including 'Golgotha , the holy hill standing above us here, bears witness to our sight: the Holy Sepulchre bears witness, and the stone which lies there to this day' (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/310110.htm); Lecture 14.23: 'you have this very place of the Resurrection; you have also the place of the Ascension towards the east' (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/310114.htm). His point is that the places confirm and strengthen faith; he does not say God is absent elsewhere. He was still bishop when Gregory of Nyssa visited and wrote the opposite view.

stances.summary: Seeing the very place where a saint suffered does real good to the soul. People rightly cross seas to see it and kiss the ground, and I long to see Paul's chains and embrace his tomb.
stances.quote: but from the sight of Job's dunghill, one may derive every kind of benefit, yea, much divine wisdom and consolation, in order to patience. Therefore to this day many undertake a long pilgrimage, even across the sea, hastening from the extremities of the earth, as far as Arabia, that they may see that dunghill; and having beheld it, may kiss the land
stances.translation: W.R.W. Stephens (revising the Oxford Library of the Fathers), NPNF first series vol. 9, 1889
stances.context: Repeated in several places, so strength 2. Homily 8 on Ephesians: 'Would that I could be at this moment in that very spot, (for the bonds are said to be still in existence,) to behold and admire those men, for their love of Christ. Would that I could behold the chains' (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230108.htm). Homily 32 on Romans: 'I love Rome even for this' because Paul and Peter lie there, and he wishes 'to throw myself round' Paul's body 'and be riveted to the tomb, and to see the dust of that body' (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210232.htm; the page prints Greek words and Bible references inside the sentence). He also teaches that true worshippers 'confine not their service by place' (Homily 33 on John, on John 4:21), but that passage is about the Jewish and Samaritan temples, not Christian pilgrimage. No surviving line of his argues against pilgrimage.

stances.summary: People go to Jerusalem for one reason: to see and touch the places where Christ was bodily present, and to say they have worshipped where His feet stood. To bring home a little dust of those places, or a splinter of the Cross, is a blessing.
stances.quote: For no other longing sweeps people off to Jerusalem than to see and touch the places where Christ was present in the body, and to be able to declare from their own harvest: We have entered His tabernacles and have worshipped where His feet stood.
stances.translation: own close rendering from the Latin of Hartel, CSEL 29 (1894); the only full English (Walsh, 1966 to 1967) is under copyright
stances.original: non enim alter affectus homines ad Hierosolymam rapit, nisi ut loca, in quibus corporaliter praesens fuit Christus, uideant atque contingant possintque et de suo fructu edicere: introiuimus in tabernacula eius et adorauimus ubi steterunt pedes eius.
stances.context: The url is the OCR text of Hartel's edition: the Latin there is broken across lines with hyphens ('Hierosoly- mam') and has the editor's '(ut)' and OCR slips ('Ohristus', 'saltern'); the original field is de-hyphenated and corrected. The next sentence continues: 'so if it is a devout desire to see the places where Christ entered, suffered, rose again and from which He went up, and to take and keep a little dust from those places or some splinter of the wood of the Cross, it is a blessing' (si ergo religiosa cupiditas est loca uidere ... benedictio est). His argument then moves on: a living old man, Valgius, rescued from shipwreck by God, is even more worth seeing than the places. Paulinus never went to Jerusalem himself; Jerome's Letter 58 was written to put him off. Instead, from 395 he settled at the tomb of St Felix at Nola, built a pilgrim complex there and wrote a poem for the crowds at every yearly feast. Augustine sent two disputants to that same shrine (Letter 78). Written in the early 400s.

stances.summary: We come near to God by love and good living, not by changing places, since He is everywhere. Yet God chooses to do His wonders at some holy places and not others, and no one can say why.
stances.quote: But in regard to the answers to prayer which are visible to men, who can search out His reasons for appointing some places rather than others to be the scene of miraculous interpositions? To many the holiness of the place in which the body of the blessed Felix is buried is well known
stances.translation: J.G. Cunningham, NPNF first series vol. 1, 1887
stances.original: Verumtamen ad ista quae hominibus visibiliter nota sunt, quis potest eius consilium perscrutari, quare in aliis locis haec miracula fiant, in aliis non fiant? Multis enim notissima est sanctitas loci, ubi beati Felicis Nolensis corpus conditum est
stances.work: Letter 78, to the clergy, elders and people of Hippo
stances.context: A deliberate middle view, stated from both sides. The sentence just before the quote: 'God is everywhere, it is true, and He that made all things is not contained or confined to dwell in any place; and He is to be worshipped in spirit and in truth by His true worshippers'. He had sent a priest and a monk, each accusing the other, to the shrine of St Felix at Nola, where God might reveal the guilty one. The principle side, in his own words: 'For it is not by change of place that we can come nearer to Him who is in every place, but by the cultivation of pure desires and virtuous habits' (On Christian Doctrine 1.10, begun 396 or 397, trans. J.F. Shaw, NPNF first series vol. 2, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/12021.htm; Latin 'Non enim ad eum qui ubique praesens est locis movemur, sed bono studio bonisque moribus'). And in a later sermon (usually dated 417): 'do not conceive of long journeyings; where you believe, there you come. For unto Him, who is everywhere we come by love, not by sailing' (Sermon 131.2, NPNF numbering Sermon 81 on the New Testament, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/160381.htm); there he is speaking of coming to Christ by faith, not of pilgrimage as such. On burial beside martyrs he says the dead are helped 'not by the place of its dead body, but by that which springs from memory of the place' (On the Care of the Dead 7, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1316.htm). Late in life he gave more weight to healings at martyrs' shrines (City of God 22.8, about 426: 'For even now miracles are wrought in the name of Christ, whether by His sacraments or by the prayers or relics of His saints'), and in his Retractations he corrected his earlier remark that such miracles had ceased. On nearness to God by love, not place, he never changed.

stances.summary: God does work wonders at the tombs and caves of the saints. But the stronger faith is the one that knows the saints hear us even where their bodies do not lie, and loves Christ without needing His bodily presence.
stances.quote: But he whose mind is fixed in God, hath so much the greater merit of his faith in that he both knoweth that they rest not there in body, and yet be there present to hear our prayers.
stances.translation: P.W. (1608), revised and edited by Edmund G. Gardner, The Dialogues of Saint Gregory, 1911
stances.context: The page wraps lines, so match with whitespace normalised. Same chapter, just before: Benedict, buried at Monte Cassino, 'also in that cave in which he first dwelled, even to this very time, worketh miracles, if the faith of them that pray requireth the same', and a wandering madwoman who slept one night in Benedict's cave at Subiaco woke cured. Gregory also affirms that 'Where the holy martyrs lie in their bodies, there is no doubt, Peter, but that they are able to work many miracles'. Then he explains that greater miracles happen where the bodies are not, for the sake of weak faith, and closes with Christ's word 'If I do not depart, the Comforter will not come', glossed as 'except you give over [cease] to love my carnal presence, never will you learn to affect me with true spiritual love.' So he honours holy places but ranks the faith that does not need them higher. Written 593 to 594.

stances.summary: At the newly found bodies of the martyrs, God's grace is at work: the possessed are freed and the sick are healed by touching what belonged to the saints.
stances.quote: Ye have heard, nay, yourselves have seen, many cleansed from evil spirits; many also, after touching with their hands the garments of the saints, delivered from the infirmities under which they suffered
stances.translation: Library of the Fathers (Oxford), Letters of S. Ambrose, 1881 (translator not named)
stances.context: About a martyrs' shrine and relics, not a journey to the Holy Land, so strength 1 for this claim. Ambrose found the bodies of Gervasius and Protasius in Milan in 386; 'The people flocked thither in crowds throughout the whole of those two days', a blind man was healed, and he placed the relics under the altar of his new basilica: 'Bring these victorious victims to the spot where Christ is the sacrifice.' Augustine, then in Milan, reports the same events (Confessions 9.7) and later cites them (Letter 78). Ambrose's funeral speech for Theodosius (395) also praises Helena's journey to Golgotha and her finding of the Cross, but no pre-1929 English exists for it and it was not checked here.

stances.summary: Believers now come from every part of the world to Jerusalem, not for the old Temple, but to learn from the ruined city and to worship on the Mount of Olives, where the Lord's feet stood.
stances.quote: believers in Christ all congregate from all parts of the world, not as of old time because of the glory of Jerusalem, nor that they may worship in the ancient Temple at Jerusalem, but they rest there that they may learn both about the city being taken and devastated as the prophets foretold, and that they may worship at the Mount of Olives opposite to the city
stances.translation: W.J. Ferrar, The Proof of the Gospel, SPCK, 1920
stances.context: Not in the candidate pool. Written around 314 to 320, before Constantine's churches, so it shows pilgrims were already coming. The page wraps lines, so match with whitespace normalised. He presents it as a fulfilment of prophecy (Zechariah 14, Ezekiel 11) and stresses that Christians do not come for the Temple; the purpose is learning and worship at the place of the Ascension. Eusebius was sympathetic to Arius early on but signed the creed of Nicaea. Earlier travel he records is about learning, not devotion: Melito of Sardis went 'East and came to the place where these things were preached and done' to learn the Old Testament canon (Church History 4.26), and Alexander came to Jerusalem around 212 'in consequence of a vow and for the sake of information in regard to its places' (Church History 6.11, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/250106.htm; that one is Eusebius's report, not Alexander's words).

stances.summary: The mature Christian honours God in every place and all through life, not in one chosen place or temple or on special days. The Church is the gathering of God's people, not a place.
stances.quote: Whence not in a specified place, or selected temple, or at certain festivals and on appointed days, but during his whole life, the Gnostic in every place, even if he be alone by himself, and wherever he has any of those who have exercised the like faith, honours God
stances.context: Use with care: written around 200, before Christian pilgrimage to holy places existed, and aimed at pagan temple religion, not at Christian pilgrims. 'Gnostic' is his word for the mature Christian, not the heretics. Same book, chapter 5: 'For it is not now the place, but the assemblage of the elect, that I call the Church.' Clearly held, but he never addresses Christian holy places, so strength 1.

stances.summary: Do not travel to see a holy man. What you need to see is how he lives, and you can know that without making the journey.
stances.quote: For it is these which it is necessary for thee to see.
stances.translation: E.A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907 (from the Syriac)
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge's Syriac collection)
stances.location: Budge vol. 2, Sayings of the Holy Fathers, no. 253 (the story of the Roman lady who sailed to see Arsenius)
stances.context: The url is OCR text; its quotation marks are garbled (a stray '44' often stands for an opening quote), so only this one clean line is given as the quote. The fuller passage, cleaned: a rich Roman virgin sailed to Egypt to see him and he rebuked her: 'Hast thou not heard about my works, and that I am a sinner? For it is these which it is necessary for thee to see. How didst thou dare to travel hither by ship? Didst thou not know that thou wast a woman, and that it was incumbent upon thee not to go forth anywhere? Wouldst thou go back to Rome and make a boast to the women [there] that thou hast seen Arsenius, and dost thou wish to make the sea into a road whereby women shall come unto me?' Cautions: it concerns a journey to a holy person, not a holy place, though visiting desert saints was a main form of pilgrimage (Egeria and Paula did it); the rebuke is bound up with his refusal to see women, and in the story the archbishop explains it that way and assures her that Arsenius will pray for her soul. The same story is in the Greek alphabetical collection under Arsenius; modern translations of that are copyrighted.

splits_fathers: Real voices exist on both sides, but most who wrote on it after Constantine built the Jerusalem churches (from the 320s) were in favour: Cyril of Jerusalem, Egeria, Paula, Jerome (most of his life), Paulinus of Nola, Chrysostom, Ambrose, with Eusebius noting pilgrims even earlier. The sharpest 'no' is Gregory of Nyssa's letter On Pilgrimages. Jerome in Letter 58 and Augustine argue that nearness to God is by love and good living, not by place, but neither condemns holy places: Jerome lived in Bethlehem and Augustine sent people to a shrine. The desert fathers distrusted travel in general (Arsenius; anonymous sayings about wandering 'from place to place'). Before the 300s, pilgrimage as devotion barely existed: Clement and Origen put holiness in the soul and the gathered Church, and early journeys (Melito, Alexander, Origen) were for study. Almost nobody on either side said God is absent from ordinary places, and almost nobody on the 'no' side said holy places are worthless. The real divide is whether the place itself adds anything, or only the heart you bring to it.
splits_people_today: As worded ('can bring you closer'), most people today would agree. Catholics and Orthodox practise pilgrimage widely (the Holy Land, Rome, Lourdes, Fatima, Mount Athos, the Camino). Many evangelicals who would never say a place holds grace still take Holy Land tours that 'bring the Bible to life', and would agree that such a trip can deepen faith. Many 'spiritual but not religious' people value sacred sites and long walks. The firm 'no' today comes mainly from Reformed and other Protestants who hold that God is equally present everywhere and that pilgrimage adds nothing (the Reformers attacked it), and from secular people who think any closeness felt is only psychological. So the claim is fairly one-sided today. A wording that asks whether the place itself adds something, or whether it is better to stay put and seek God where you are, would split people more evenly. That is also where the Fathers really divide.

misattributions.line: The world is a book, and those who do not travel read only one page.
misattributions.truth: Not found anywhere in Augustine. The earliest known form is Richard Lassels, The Voyage of Italy (1670), who credited only the idea of the world as 'a great book' to Augustine and added the line about staying home himself; later writers credited the whole sentence to Augustine (Quote Investigator, 25 September 2025, https://quoteinvestigator.com/2025/09/25/world-book/).

misattributions.line: Solvitur ambulando (It is solved by walking).
misattributions.attributed_to: Augustine of Hippo (often used on pilgrimage and Camino sites)
misattributions.truth: No Augustine source is known. The story behind it is Diogenes the Cynic answering Zeno's paradoxes of motion by getting up and walking (reported by Simplicius). A claim online that Augustine wrote 'Ambulando solvitur ista quaestio' in his Literal Commentary on Genesis is false: the only 'ambulando' in that work (8.21.41) describes how a foot moves when walking. It has nothing to do with pilgrimage.

misattributions.line: The court of heaven is as open from Britain as from Jerusalem.
misattributions.truth: Genuine (Letter 58.3), but this is a modern paraphrase. The public-domain NPNF wording is 'Access to the courts of heaven is as easy from Britain as it is from Jerusalem; for the kingdom of God is within you.' Quote that wording.

misattributions.line: We come to God not by sailing but by loving.
misattributions.truth: Genuine, but often misapplied as a verdict on pilgrimage. It is Sermon 131.2 (NPNF Sermon 81 on the New Testament), where Augustine is explaining that we come to Christ by believing and loving, as the Father draws us (John 6:44). NPNF wording: 'For unto Him, who is everywhere we come by love, not by sailing.' His direct statement of the principle is On Christian Doctrine 1.10.

notes: 1. Capitals: the NPNF and other pages sometimes print pronouns for God in lower case (Gregory of Nyssa's Letter 17: 'the God who gave us life'; Budge's text is inconsistent); apply the site's capitals rule when displaying. 2. Several urls wrap lines or are OCR text (tertullian.org pages for Gregory the Great and Eusebius; archive.org OCR for Budge, CSEL 29, CSEL 54, CSEL 55): match quotes with whitespace normalised. The Paulinus quote is my own rendering, so only its Latin can be checked against the OCR, and that needs de-hyphenation. 3. Voices checked but NOT made stances: Moses the Black, 'Get thee gone, and sit in thy cell, and thy cell shall teach thee everything' (Budge vol. 2, no. 62), is about staying in one's own place, not about holy places, so it is weak evidence at most; an anonymous elder in Budge (no. 195, OCR cleaned) warns that 'we go from place to place, and expect to find some spot where Satan is not ... For the kingdom of heaven is within you'. Origen visited the Jordan sites 'to enquire as to the footsteps of Jesus and His disciples, and of the prophets' (Commentary on John 6.24, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/101506.htm): scholarly research, not a claim about nearness to God. Budge also has a story (no. 599) of an anonymous monk to whom Christ appeared in a dream in the Church of the Resurrection. 4. Not verified, so not used: Athanasius's Letter to the Virgins who went to Jerusalem to pray and returned (Syriac only; edited by Lebon, Le Museon 41, 1928; English only in Brakke 1995, copyrighted). Secondary summaries say he shares their love of the places but consoles them that one who lives in holiness carries Jerusalem within. Athanasius is in the pool; if he is needed, someone must read Lebon's Syriac or French. Basil's and Gregory of Nyssa's homilies at martyrs' shrines (the Forty Martyrs, Theodore) likely show them honouring shrines, but no pre-1929 English was found and they were not checked. 5. No source was found in the pool for Ignatius, Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Perpetua, Hippolytus, Cyprian, Novatian, Lactantius, Antony (Jerome says only that he never saw Jerusalem), Ephrem, Hilary, Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Macrina, Syncletica, Poemen, Evagrius, Pelagius, Cassian, Martin, Benedict, Boethius, John Climacus or Isaac the Syrian. Beware Climacus: his Step 3 is often titled 'On exile' or 'On pilgrimage', but it means leaving home as an ascetic, not visiting holy places. 6. Not patristic, do not use as a Father: 'Qui multum peregrinantur, raro sanctificantur' ('those who travel much are seldom made holy') is Thomas a Kempis, Imitation of Christ 1.23 (15th century); the verse beginning 'To go to Rome' is a 9th-century Old Irish marginal verse. 7. Vigilantius, a Gallic priest who opposed vigils at martyrs' tombs, is known only through Jerome's attack on him (Against Vigilantius, 406), so his view cannot be recorded in his own words. 8. Best pairing for a reveal: Gregory of Nyssa ('Change of place does not effect any drawing nearer unto God') against Jerome's Letter 47 or Paula ('here will I dwell for this spot has my Saviour chosen'). Jerome's own reversal between Letters 47 and 58 is a good 'even the Fathers argued with themselves' note.
